statement: Which value of x satisfies the equation x + the square root of (x + 6) = 14?

choices.misconception: I dropped the square root sign and solved x + x + 6 = 14.
I found that the number under the square root is 16 and gave that instead of x.
I squared both sides, solved the quadratic and kept the root 19 without checking it in the original equation, where it gives 24.
I squared the square root and the 14 but forgot to square the x, so I solved x + x + 6 = 196.

hints: You have five candidates. Testing them may beat solving.
Substitute each choice into the left side and see which gives 14. A square root is easiest when the number under it is a perfect square, so look for those choices first.
For x = 10 the number under the square root is 16; for x = 19 it is 25. Work out the left side for both.

solutions.reliable: Test the choices. x = 10 gives 10 + the square root of 16 = 10 + 4 = 14, which works. The others fail: for example x = 19 gives 19 + 5 = 24, and x = 4 gives 4 plus the square root of 10, which is not even whole. So x = 10. The transferable idea: when the choices are concrete numbers and the algebra invites mistakes, substituting them is fast and can never produce a false root.
solutions.elegant: The algebra confirms it: the square root of (x + 6) = 14 - x, so x + 6 = 196 - 28x + x squared, which gives x squared - 29x + 190 = 0, that is (x - 10)(x - 19) = 0. Only x = 10 survives, because 14 - x cannot be negative.

whyOnTest: Back-solving beats squaring here: squaring creates a false root, 19, which sits among the choices to catch anyone who does not check.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
